Evidence / CLM-045
Evidence record

A successful cash payment is not yet durable financial use

When was it measured or observed?Evidence published 2023–2026; the pilot material dates from May 2024, and the reference period of the 45,460 figure is not recorded here
Who or what does it apply to?Local, programme and project populations as each source defines them
Report an error

01What does this evidence establish?

World Bank/G2Px material (May 2024) describes an eight-district digital-payment pilot within Yemen's unconditional cash-transfer programme, reported to have benefited 45,460 recipients, with an emphasis on payments into fully functional accounts and recipient choice. As reported by programme partners, this indicates delivery and exposure to a formal digital service. Yemen evidence can support several links from cash delivery through usability, resilience and local financial relationships, but it does not yet establish persistent post-transfer bank-account or e-wallet use. Beneficiaries, registrations, identities and opened accounts are not measures of durable use. The pilot sat inside a much larger programme. UNICEF, which implemented the World Bank-funded unconditional cash transfer programme with the Social Fund for Development, announced in October 2024 that more than 1.43 million families were receiving assistance in its 18th payment cycle, which ran to mid-October, at payment sites, through mobile teams and home outreach, and in an e-wallet pilot; the figure is the cycle's announced reach, not a count of confirmed payments. In December 2024 it announced that the 19th cycle, starting on 11 December 2024 at fixed payment sites, marked the end of the programme in its then-current form. The pilot's 45,460 recipients and the programme's 1.43 million families are different counts, and one is not a share of the other; a family reached by a payment cycle does not thereby hold an account. Two Cash Consortium of Yemen studies of recipients of the Consortium partners' humanitarian cash assistance, a programme separate from the unconditional cash transfer, in sub-districts that the studies place in areas under the internationally recognized government, point to debt repayment as a common use of transfers. In a survey of recipient households in Ad-Dali and Ja’ar in January 2024 (291 and 209 interviews), posted online by its host in November 2024, 40% reported debt repayment among their regular expenses in the 30 days before the interview: about 47% of households that had received a transfer in those 30 days and about 30% of those that had not. In a 2026 study comparing three and six monthly transfers in Ja’ar, “debts are paid off” was one of the two most common answers to which part of the household economy improved most at the endline in November 2025 (one answer allowed): 60% of the 45 households that received six transfers gave it, and 40% of the 107 that received three. In the 2024 study, 11 of 21 business owners who answered in Ad-Dali and 10 of 21 in Ja’ar said that fewer customers bought on credit when cash assistance was distributed. These are local samples of aid recipients and business owners, not national estimates, and the business owners' answers are counts of interviews, not credit volumes. They are one reason why immediate cash-out is not, by itself, a sign that a transfer failed.

02What does it measure?

This record sets out a measurement gap between successful delivery of a cash transfer and continued financial use after it; its only figure is the pilot's reported number of recipients.

03How current is it?

The latest evidence in this record was published in 2026; the pilot material dates from May 2024. The programme the pilot belonged to has run no payment cycle since January 2025, for lack of funds, according to the World Bank's implementation report on the emergency social protection project that finances it (ESPECRP), archived on 30 June 2026; the project is due to close on 31 December 2026. The Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project, whose financing agreement was signed on 2 September 2026, builds on ESPECRP's delivery systems but is designed to pay a different benefit, six months of cash for nutrition to pregnant women and mothers of children under two; it does not restore the unconditional transfers. The record should not be read as describing later programme reach or use unless newer evidence is published.

04What this evidence does not establish

Cash-transfer beneficiaries, village savings and loan associations (VSLAs), identity targets and opened accounts are not measures of durable financial use. The 45,460 figure is a programme-reported number of recipients, not a count of people who kept using an account. The FMIIP appraisal document (May 2025) reports, for a pilot it does not identify with this one, that by the end of payment cycle 18 (16 September–17 October 2024) 10,761 wallets had been opened with cash transfers paid into them, with take-up of 40% to 70% across pilot districts; it differs in document, date and unit, and no ratio to 45,460 is drawn. A Cash Consortium of Yemen study (2026) compared three and six monthly transfers using programme data, with no randomised design and no group of households that received no assistance: the extra three transfers brought modest further gains in food security and less negative coping, and savings could not be compared, because only three households, all of them on six transfers, reported putting any money aside. The appraisal document of the Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project (June 2026) reports from the cash-transfer programme's monitoring that “high transaction costs and long distances to financial service points severely impeded e-wallet uptake”, and plans for recipients to cash out through agents hired by financial service providers, given the scarcity of bank branches and ATMs. On cash-out, a Cash Consortium of Yemen report of May 2026 says that most multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA: the humanitarian cash programmes the report covers, not the unconditional cash transfer, which has run no payment cycle since January 2025) was disbursed through microfinance banks as vouchers that recipients exchange at local agents of financial service providers and, citing one interview with an MPCA programme manager in April 2026, that during the Ramadan and Eid holiday period agents often lacked enough cash, with waits of four to five hours. It reports that funds were released only in denominations of YER 100 and 200 and, citing the same interview, that an e-wallet pilot disbursed funds without problems or delays. These are reported observations, some of them from a single interview. The paragraph names no programme or area, though the report frames the liquidity crisis as affecting areas under the internationally recognized government, rural recipients most, and says that liquidity problems for MPCA programmes eased after the period of high demand. The e-wallet result concerns disbursement, not whether recipients could then obtain cash, which the report itself calls unclear.

Limits of the measure

Evidence exists for several intermediate links; durable use of an account or wallet after the transfer remains unobserved.

06Method and verification detail

Detail for reproducing or challenging this record without changing what it means.

How was it produced?

A synthesis of programme and research evidence on each step from cash delivery to continued use, including World Bank/G2Px material on the pilot; no national prevalence figure is constructed.

When does this record change?

This record is updated when an authoritative source is revised or replaced, a newer comparable observation becomes available, the definition, population or method changes, or the conditions for public use change.

How can I verify it?

This record is drawn from the source(s) listed on this page. Open a source record to reach the original document, and check that the definition, period, population and geography match what is stated here.

How should this record be read?

Read this evidence within the definition, population or group covered, calculation base where relevant, period, geography and method shown on the page. Before reusing or comparing it, check the source, limitations, evidence date and correction history. If a value or source link is unavailable, the page says so rather than filling the gap by inference.
